title: [tuner] Fail a task as soon as its worker process exits
body:
## Summary

Fixes #5840.

A GPU memory fault aborts the worker process, so its task never returns a result. `mp_tuner` only noticed at the per-task timeout (1800 s by default through `base_tuner`), or never when called without a timeout, and then counted it as a GPU hang.

This PR records the PID of the worker that starts each task, next to the existing start timestamp. When a poll times out and that PID no longer exists, the task is failed right away and the pool restarts, the same way the existing `AcceleratorError` path handles it.

## Repro (MI325X, main a75ba53)

Five fake tasks go through `mp_tuner(..., fast_mode=True)`. Task 2 calls `os.abort()`, which is how the HSA runtime ends a process on a memory fault.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `timeout=None` | never returns (killed after 150 s) | returns after **23.8 s**; task 2 counted as a crash |
| `timeout=60` | 73.3 s; task 2 counted as `Timeouts (GPU hang): 1` | **23.7 s**; `Crashes (memory fault): 1` |

The other four tasks return the same results in both.

## Real tuning run

`gemm_a8w8_blockscale_tune.py --libtype both --splitK --mp 2` on 21 gfx942 shapes, default timeout, 40-minute cap. The CKTile candidates for these shapes fault repeatedly on gfx942:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| worker faults handled in 40 min | 1 (via the 1800 s timeout) | 144 |
| time spent waiting on a dead worker | most of the run | none |

Neither run finishes the batch within 40 minutes, because every CK-Tile split-K candidate on these shapes kills its worker and each kill still costs a pool restart (about 16 s).

## Why the workers die

On gfx942, CK issues bf16 atomic adds as `global_atomic_pk_add_bf16`, which skips the buffer range check. A split-K GEMM with M not a multiple of the tile M therefore adds past the end of the output and faults whenever that memory is unmapped. The fix is in ROCm/rocm-libraries#12594. With that fix and this PR together, the same 21-shape batch finishes in 80 s on 7 GPUs (`--mp 7`) with no faults. Adding #5847 as well, it also tunes on a single GPU (`--mp 1`) in 705 s with no failed shapes, and 5 of the 21 winners are CK-Tile kernels (max errRatio 0.0002). This PR still matters for any other fault: without it, a dead worker costs the full task timeout, or hangs the tuner when no timeout is set.

## Test plan

- [x] New unit tests: `_task_worker_exited` on a reaped PID, a live PID and a queued task; worker PID recorded when a task starts; reset clears PIDs
- [x] `op_tests/tuning_tests/test_mp_tuner_logic.py` passes
- [x] Repro and real run above

Found by [Hyperloom](https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Hyperloom); reviewed and measured by hand.
Hyperloom was optimizing `Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8` when its GEMM tuning step hung.

title: [CK] blockscale split-K: pick the pipeline from the per-split loop count
body:
## Summary

`gemm_a8w8_blockscale_cktile` picks the pipeline variant (`has_hot_loop`, `tail_num`) from the loop count of the full K. With split-K, each split only runs `K / (k_batch * K_Tile)` loops. When a split is short (two K loops), the selected variant does not match the loops it actually runs, and the output is silently wrong.

This PR computes the loop count per split, the same way the other CK-Tile launchers in aiter already do: `ck_deepgemm`, `ck_tile_gemm_moe_2stages` and `cktile_gemm_a8w8_bpreshuffle` all use `k_grain = k_batch * K_Tile`.

## Results (MI325X, gfx942)

Public `gemm_a8w8_blockscale_cktile` with the default kernel (K_Tile 128), split-K output compared against split-K 0, fraction of mismatched elements:

| M, N, K | splitK (splits) | loops per split | before | after |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 8, 256, 512 | 1 (2) | 2 | 0.69 | 0 |
| 8, 256, 1024 | 2 (4) | 2 | 0.87 | 0 |
| 32, 512, 2048 | 3 (8) | 2 | 0.97 | 0 |

Every CK-Tile tuning candidate on gfx942 (80 instances × splitK 0–3 × 8 shapes, M from 1 to 16384, (N, K) = (128, 6144) and (256, 4096); 2560 runs), compared against a torch reference:

- Wrong results (errRatio > 0.05) drop from 80 to 0. All 80 were splits with two K loops.
- The 224 rejected candidates and every splitK = 0 result are unchanged.
- The remaining split-K results differ only by atomic-add ordering (errRatio at most 0.008).

The tuner already rejected these candidates through errRatio, so no tuned config was affected. Direct split-K calls with short splits were.

## Test plan

- [x] `op_tests/test_gemm_a8w8_blockscale.py`: `test_splitk_correctness` now asserts on the error ratio and covers three shapes with two K loops per split. Before this change the new cases fail (`cktile_err=0.8716`); after it, all cases pass. The existing cases pass either way.

body:
## Motivation

Upstream the DSV4.1 Flash EP4 a8w4 FMoE rows carried by sgl-project/sglang#39186. Without this table the exact gfx950 shape falls back to heuristic FlyDSL kernels. Removing the downstream CSV reduced performance in the operator comparison below, so it is restored downstream while this PR is reviewed.

## Technical Details

- Add 12 unique tuning rows under `aiter/configs/model_configs/`, plus the corresponding untuned shape input.
- Shape: gfx950 / 256 CUs, model_dim=5120, inter_dim=2304, 96 local experts, topk=5, Silu, bf16 input/output, FP8 activations and FP4 weights with per-1x32 quantization, interleaved gate/up weights, no stage-1 routing weight.
- Token buckets: 1, 2, 4, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 4096, 8192, 16384.
- Add `op_tests/op_benchmarks/bench_dsv41_fmoe.py` for a reproducible default-versus-tuned graph comparison. It excludes the candidate CSV from the baseline even when running from this branch and preserves the other model tables.
- All 12 rows survive normal `AITER_CONFIG_FMOE_FILE` merging; no matching shape keys exist in the current shipped model/default tables.

The rows and their `us` / error columns are imported from the original downstream tuning data; those columns are historical, not the measurements below. This PR is based on `main` at `0138f88b2`.

## Test Plan

For the measurements below, apply the stage-1 synchronization fix in #5561 to this branch, then run:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 TRITON_HIP_USE_ASYNC_COPY=0 \
AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=0 AITER_FLYDSL_FORCE_REDUCE=1 \
python op_tests/op_benchmarks/bench_dsv41_fmoe.py \
  --csv aiter/configs/model_configs/a8w4_tuned_fmoe_dsv41_flash_gfx950.csv \
  --tokens 1 32 128 512 4096
```

The benchmark uses seeded synthetic FP4 weights and bf16 activations. Timing is the median of five GPU-event measurements, each covering 100 graph replays after warmup. Both configurations use the same synchronization fix and inputs. The Triton environment flag is a local toolchain workaround.

## Test Result

MI350X VF (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.4, PyTorch 2.11.0+rocm7.2:

| Tokens | Default (us) | Tuned (us) | Speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 48.37 | 37.44 | 1.29x |
| 32 | 290.40 | 267.83 | 1.08x |
| 128 | 349.43 | 320.22 | 1.09x |

| 4096 | 1411.56 | 1248.79 | 1.13x |

A separate one-token smoke rerun measured 47.17 -> 37.61 us (1.25x). Black, Ruff, CSV uniqueness and normal config merge checks pass.

**Numerical limitation:** the benchmark checks finiteness and reports differences; it is not an independent accuracy oracle. Tuned versus default maximum absolute differences were 0.0273-0.0410 on the synthetic inputs. An initial strict comparison at 32 tokens (`atol=0.02, rtol=0.05`) rejected 13/163840 elements. The two paths differ in intermediate quantization/reduction, so this requires review rather than asserting equivalence.

**Not executed:** a fresh exhaustive tuning sweep, full-model accuracy/throughput, the other seven buckets, or other architectures. Keep this PR in draft until numerical tolerances, all buckets, and the paired synchronization fix are reviewed. These operator timings are not an end-to-end model speedup.

A second comparison on the installed SGLang-pinned AITER `4ad998328` also favored the CSV: M=1: 43.05 -> 37.17 us (1.16x), M=32: 291.22 -> 262.54 us (1.11x), M=128: 343.24 -> 316.97 us (1.08x), M=512: 419.93 -> 399.23 us (1.05x), M=4096: 1359.34 -> 1239.05 us (1.10x). title: [CI] Add PRs to the AITER-triton Kernels board without relying on labels
body:
## Motivation

The AITER-triton Kernels board (https://github.com/orgs/ROCm/projects/232) fills only through the `Triton/Gluon` label today: the board's auto-add rule matches labeled PRs, and the label comes from `pr-title-tags.yaml`. That leaves two holes. The `no-auto-title` opt-out skipped the label sync entirely, so an opted-out Triton PR never reached the board, and nothing puts work on the board when the label is missing for any other reason. The Triton kernels team also wants everything assigned to a team member on the board, whatever it touches (CI, docs, config, ...).

## Technical Details

- `pr-title-tags.yaml`: `no-auto-title` now only leaves the title alone. Component labels are always synced.
- `pr-welcome-comment.yaml`: the CI guide comment says so too.
- New `aiter-triton-board.yaml`: on PR events (`opened`, `reopened`, `ready_for_review`, `synchronize`, `assigned`, `labeled`) and issue events (`opened`, `reopened`, `assigned`, `labeled`) it adds the item to the board when any of these hold: assigned to a member of `@ROCm/triton_kernels_team` (roster inline, GitHub offers no team filter for projects), the PR diff touches Triton/Gluon paths (same list as `isTriton` in `pr-title-tags.yaml`), or it carries the `Triton/Gluon` label. Drafts wait for `ready_for_review`. Adding an item that is already on the board is a no-op, so re-evaluating on every event is harmless. `pull_request_target` with no checkout, same pattern as the title workflow.
- Token: `actions/create-github-app-token@v1` with the existing `AITER_CI_APP_ID` / `AITER_CI_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` secrets, then `actions/add-to-project@v2`.
- The job is gated on the repository variable `AITER_TRITON_BOARD_ADD == 'true'`, so merging this changes nothing until it is switched on.

**Enabling it (org / repo admin):**
1. Grant the AITER CI GitHub App the organization permission **Projects: Read & write** and accept the new permission on the ROCm installation.
2. Add the repository variable `AITER_TRITON_BOARD_ADD` = `true` (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables).

The board's own auto-add rules (`label:Triton/Gluon`, and assignee in the team roster) keep working alongside this as a second path.

Tuning for large head_size=512 attn_2d tuning for Strix Halo, of fp8/bf16 KV cache.

## Motivation
vLLM's default `TRITON_ATTN` backend doesn't offer optimal tuning config for gfx1151, and there isn't per-arch tunning opportunity.

## Test Result

### Kernel-level, bf16 KV / bf16 Q

| kv_len | q_len | block | TRITON_ATTN (ms) | AITER before (ms) | AITER tuned (ms) | tuned vs before (improvement) | tuned vs TRITON_ATTN (improvement) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32,768 | 32,768 | 16 | 12830.31 | 4215.41 | 2211.04 | 1.91× | 5.80× |
| 32,768 | 32,768 | 64 | 11119.52 | 4050.21 | 2265.70 | 1.79× | 4.91× |

### Kernel-level, fp8 KV / bf16 Q

| kv_len | TRITON_ATTN (ms) | AITER before (ms) | AITER tuned (ms) | tuned vs before (improvement) | tuned vs TRITON_ATTN (improvement) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32,768 | 1452.3 | 971.8 | 615.1 | 1.58× | 2.36× |
| 60,000 | 2723.7 | 1789.8 | 1193.2 | 1.50× | 2.28× |

### Model-level, `vllm bench serve`

32768-in / 32-out, `--max-num-seqs 1`, `--max-concurrency 1`, `--num-prompts 4`

| backend | KV | Median TTFT (ms) | Median TPOT (ms) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| TRITON_ATTN | bf16 | 146005.21 | 73.58 |
| ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN | bf16 | 20117.60 | 50.59 |
| TRITON_ATTN | fp8 | 164764.79 | 85.09 |
| ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN | fp8 | 63824.95 | 70.63 |

| comparison | Median TTFT improvement | Median TPOT improvement|
|---|---:|---:|
| tuned vs TRITON_ATTN, bf16 KV | 7.26× | 1.45× |
| tuned vs TRITON_ATTN, fp8 KV | 2.58× | 1.20× |

## Potential problem
Using TRITON=`3.8.0+git4cff872c.rocm10.1.0a20260811`, the compiler has an **uneven** cost upcasting fp8 to bf16/fp16, and the following local patch is required in vLLM to always pass in bf16 Q into the kernel.
`vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_aiter_unified_attn.py`, in `RocmAiterUnifiedAttentionImpl.__init__`:

```python
from vllm.platforms.rocm import on_gfx11
self.supports_quant_query_input = not on_gfx11()
```

Without it, `Attention.__init__` builds a `query_quant` whenever the KV cache is fp8 (`vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/attention.py:464-470`) and the query is quantized alongside the KV cache to fp8. 

### REASON
As gfx1151 has no fp8 WMMA, passing in fp8 Q is not only a pure precision loss, but also causes the kernel to regress up to 4 times. The Triton compiler's current default WMMA upcasting dtype is fp16, not bf16. Fp16 uses a lot more cmp instructions and causes the kernel to regress badly. Leaving Q in bf16, then inside kernel do `K_load.to(Q.dtype)`, `V_load.to(Q.dtype)` explicitly uses bf16 and bypasses the compiler problem. This is what the above table measurements are based on.

For conclusion, this is a pure use case problem, and this PR stays valid. Investigation into Triton compiler's RDNA3 fp8 upcasting dtype (fp16/bf16) is ongoing.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [FlyDSL] [GDN] Segmented affine-scan K5 for long prefills
body:
## Motivation

Stock FlyDSL K5 assigns one program per `(sequence, head, V tile)` and walks 64-token chunks serially. A single 16k Qwen3.8 TP8 sequence therefore launches only 128 programs. Segmenting recovers occupancy on long, narrow prefills without changing the prepare or `o` kernels.

### Isolated kernel (gfx950)

`python op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_gdn_segment_scan.py` — H=16, indexed varlen, idle GPU:

| seq_lens | N | stock | segmented | delta |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 8192    | 1 | 253.3 µs | 150.7 µs | −40.5% |
| 16384   | 1 | 507.2 µs | 275.6 µs | −45.7% |
| 32768   | 1 | 952.3 µs | 504.4 µs | −47.0% |
| 16384×2 | 2 | 575.7 µs | 492.0 µs | −14.5% |
| 8192×4  | 4 | 400.6 µs | 487.9 µs | +21.8% |

The N=4 row is why the dispatch gate keeps packed batches on FlyDSL.

## Technical Details

The per-chunk hidden-state update is affine in the incoming state: for `h` shaped `[V, K]`,

```text
h' = h @ A + b
```

A long sequence is split into segments of `ceil(total_chunks / 16)` chunks. Each segment is an independent affine map, recovered without materializing a dense operator per chunk:

1. **Summaries.** Run the same recurrence over each segment twice in one launch: start at `h=0` with `u` to get `b_seg`, and start at `h=I` with `u=0` to get `A_seg`. `A_seg` is stored as `[V, K]` with `K=V=128`.
2. **Scan.** A short sequential kernel composes those maps along the sequence and writes each segment's true incoming state, including `h0` / `state_indices` for indexed varlen pools.
3. **Output.** Rerun every segment from that state and write the stock K5 contract: chunk snapshots `h`, `v_new`, and optional final state (in-place into the SSM pool when the FlyDSL wrapper would).

`T_FLAT` is a runtime kernel argument so packed batches of different lengths do not retrigger Triton constexpr compiles. The segment kernels use `BV=64` and the scan `BV=16`, both tuned on gfx950 over the gated shapes.

The FlyDSL wrapper (`chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_flydsl_opt`) intercepts before BV selection when all of the following hold:

- `B=1`, `K=V=128`, `use_g`, not `use_gk`, head-major log2-scaled `g`, `save_new_value`
- total chunks ≥ 128 ≈ 8k tokens
- `N<=2`, or `N==3` with total chunks ≥ 512 and max seq chunks ≥ 256

Varlen needs `prefill_metadata` so CPU `seq_lens` are available. Prepare (`gdn_prepare_fwd_flydsl`) and `chunk_fwd_kernel_o_opt_vk` are unchanged.

## Test Plan

- [x] `pytest op_tests/test_gdn_segment_scan.py` on gfx950 (MI355).
- [x] Serving A/B on Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 TP8, 8×MI355X, `gdn_prefill_backend=aiter_flydsl`.
- [x] Matched 32k N=1 profiler traces.

## Test Result

### Unit tests (gfx950)

`pytest op_tests/test_gdn_segment_scan.py` — 6 passed:
| Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- |

title: [Triton/Gluon] [gfx950] pa_decode_sparse: bound split-K by wave count and tile budget (up to +22%)
body:
Bounds the split-K count in the gfx950 gluon sparse-decode driver from both sides: the launch stops
overshooting one wave of workgroups, and it stops cutting splits once each workgroup carries enough
KV tiles to pay for itself.

## What changes

`_decode_num_splits_occ` bounds the split count by `cta_cap = 2 * num_sms // base_wg`, which lets
`base_wg * splits` exceed `num_sms`. Capping that alone is not enough, though — past a point, cutting
splits stops removing overhead and starts removing parallelism. So the count is bounded by both:

```python
wave_cap = 1 << max(0, (num_sms // base_wg).bit_length() - 1)
return max(1, min(cta_cap, tiles, max(wave_cap, tiles // 4)))
```

`tiles // 4` is not a new constant — it is the split floor the `base_wg >= num_sms` branch of this
same function already uses. Only the `base_wg < num_sms` branch changes.

## Why both bounds are needed

Every split costs a fixed amount — its own partial write and its own Q re-read, both paid **inside the
attention kernel** — and that cost does not depend on how much KV the split actually covers. So the
tradeoff is per-split fixed cost against parallelism, and where it balances depends on how many KV
tiles a workgroup has to amortise it over. That is set by top-k, which is why one bound cannot do it.

An earlier revision of this PR had only `wave_cap`. Measured over 24 shapes, that is a **net
regression**:

| | wins | losses | worst | best | mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `wave_cap` only | 6 | **15** | **-43.1 %** | +22.1 % | **-7.6 %** |
| with the `tiles // 4` floor | **10** | **0** | -1.0 % | +21.9 % | **+4.2 %** |

## Measurements

MI355X / gfx950 (256 CU), DeepSeek-V4.1 decode shape: 16 heads, head_dim 512 (448 NoPE + 64 RoPE),
packed fp8 cache, 128-slot SWA window plus a top-k list per query, 8 GiB KV pool. Median of 100
samples of 4 calls in one HIP graph. Each arm runs its own `_decode_num_splits_occ` — `kv_splits` is
not pinned — so this is what merging actually gives you. Speedup against current `main`:

| queries | top-k 512 | top-k 1024 | top-k 2048 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | +0.4 % | +0.5 % | -0.2 % |
| 36 | **+15.6 %** | **+21.9 %** | **+14.8 %** |
| 48 | **+16.3 %** | +5.7 % | +6.0 % |
| 96 | +5.5 % | +8.1 % | -0.2 % |
| 126 | +5.2 % | -0.1 % | +0.3 % |
| 150 | -1.0 % | -0.5 % | +0.0 % |
| 192 | -0.3 % | -0.2 % | +0.1 % |
| 252 | +0.4 % | +0.2 % | +2.9 % |

Against a per-point sweep of `kv_splits` over {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 14, 16} at every shape, the
guarded rule lands on or within 2.5 % of the measured optimum at every one of the 24 points. The
worst cell is -1.0 %.

## Tests

`test_decode_num_splits_occ_bounds` asserts the four bounds the split count is built from — at most
`tiles`, at most `cta_cap`, at least `tiles // 4`, and within one wave where the tile floor is not
what holds the count up — plus monotonicity in top-k, over 165 shapes.

`num_sms` is patched rather than read from the device, so the body allocates nothing and the bounds
are checked at partitioned CU counts (256 / 128 / 64 / 32) rather than only whatever the runner has.
The `torch.cuda.is_available()` guard matches the in-body form the other tests in this module use.

It discriminates, and the two failing arms fail for different reasons:

```
main                4 failed   cu=32 q=1 topk=8192: 64 workgroups over 32 CUs    <- the wave ceiling
wave cap, no floor  4 failed   cu=32 q=6 topk=2048: 4 splits leaves 8 tiles/WG   <- the floor
this PR             4 passed
```

Note it fails on `main` by design: the wave ceiling is behaviour this PR introduces, so asserting it
makes the contract explicit rather than incidental. The floor assertion is the regression guard, and
it is not masked by the ceiling — the un-floored version trips the floor first.

The H=16 subset of the existing kernel test is **42 passed, 10 skipped**, identical across all three.

## Numerics

Unchanged in kind: the split count only changes how many partials the fp32 combine sums, as it
already does across the existing `cta_cap` and `tiles` bounds. Checked directly — output max
absolute deviation across every split count at every shape is **<= 9.8e-04** against the single-split
result, which is fp8 accumulation order, not a behaviour change.

`op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_pa_decode_sparse.py`, the H=16 subset: **42 passed, 10 skipped**,
identical on `main`, on the bare cap, and with the floor.

## On the mechanism

An earlier revision explained this as a partly filled second wave costing a full wave of latency. A
`rocprofv3 --kernel-trace` of the launch does not support that, and the description is corrected:

- The saving is **entirely in the attention kernel** (103 % of the delta at 48 queries, 8 -> 4
  splits); `_aiter_sparse_decode_reduce_kernel` is flat to +0.1 us. The partial write happens inside
  the attention kernel before the workgroup exits, which is where the per-split cost actually lands.
- The kernel reports `LDS_Block_Size = 0` — no static LDS — so occupancy is VGPR-limited at 128
  VGPRs, giving 4 workgroups per CU. 384 workgroups is nowhere near a wave boundary, and there is no
  partly filled second wave to pay for.

`wave_cap` is still the right shape for the upper bound; the reasoning for it is amortisation, not
wave quantisation.

## Reproducing

Measured with a standalone benchmark that calls `pa_decode_sparse` directly, independent of any
serving stack, and cross-checked against an sglang-based harness that shares no code with it. Both
agree on where the win and loss zones fall. Happy to attach the benchmark if useful.

One methodology note for anyone re-running: a first measurement process reads 3-11 % fast from cold
start, so arms must be compared back to back within one process rather than across processes.

title: [HIP] [Perf] Specialize partial tiles in two-stage custom all-reduce
body:
## Proposed modifications

1. Specialize the plain two-stage read kernel with a compile-time `has_tail` parameter.
2. Run the shared-memory loop only over complete tiles so every thread in a block executes the same number of barriers.
3. Reduce leftover packs directly with `packed_reduce`, preserving their original owner threads and output indices.
4. Preserve accumulation order and inter-device synchronization without adding a kernel launch.
5. Dispatch aligned messages to `has_tail=false`, removing tail predicates and restoring the generated aligned kernel from before #5694.
6. Keep #5694's write-mode and fused-kernel fixes intact, along with the existing naive handling of unequal rank partitions and TP6.
7. Add a Gloo-based regression with independent rank inputs, exact reference sums, and changing inputs in eager and graph execution.
8. Cover graph-owned intermediate registration, poisoned replay outputs, the reported shape and its neighbors, single-lane tails, and unequal partitions.
9. Include the flattened `(1023,512)`, `(1024,512)`, and `(1025,512)` cases in the existing default benchmark sweep, keeping the list sorted, deduplicated, and within its configured size cutoff.

## Microbenchmarks and performance comparison

This follows merged #5694 and targets current `main`; it preserves that PR's correctness fixes while specializing the plain read path. The benchmark study used four gfx950 GPUs at TP4 and a common `v0.1.22.post1` base (`b4d9154d125e09efbe098d986e40fea3549c1244`). The correct comparison baseline applied #5694's three barrier hunks (`5e77166e0c627caa109046f6469de8220efa5ba6`) to that base. These are the historical isolated-kernel measurements, not a newly timed end-to-end run of current `main`.

The study completed 44 variant runs: three alternating-order rounds for focused and broad sweeps, and five for eight additional BF16 shapes. Each case used five warmups and seven samples: 64 calls per eager sample, or 64 captured calls replayed ten times per graph sample. CUDA-event timing excludes input preparation and checking; eager results include Python launch/allocation gaps. Latencies are the median across rounds of each round's maximum per-rank sample median. Percentage changes are medians of paired within-round ratios and need not equal ratios of the displayed latencies.

For `(1025, 512)`, lower latency is better:

| Dtype | Mode | #5694 uniform loop (µs) | Tail specialization (µs) | Paired change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 | eager | 16.461 | 16.330 | -0.90% |
| BF16 | graph | 13.822 | 13.722 | -0.72% |
| FP16 | eager | 16.440 | 16.254 | -0.94% |
| FP16 | graph | 13.831 | 13.678 | -0.95% |
| FP32 | eager | 26.883 | 26.753 | -0.02% |
| FP32 | graph | 24.001 | 23.898 | -0.48% |

The full sweep includes BF16/FP16/FP32 at `(1023,512)`, `(1024,512)`, and `(1025,512)`; 43 dtype/size configurations spanning 8 KiB–8 MiB and per-rank tails of 1/63/64/65/127 packs; and BF16 `(M,2880)` for `M=120,121,127,157,160,161,256,512`. Compared with the unsafe pre-#5694 release, the proposed specialization's largest observed case-level median increases were 0.56% graph and 1.92% eager; the initial whole-message naive fallback cost about 29% on the reported BF16 graph case. The unsafe release is a historical timing reference only.

The host was shared, the other four GPUs were busy, and three to five rounds do not establish a general sub-percent regression bound. Timed graph replays reuse inputs within a sample; the separate changing-input regression provides stronger race coverage. TP8/gfx942 configurations and end-to-end model throughput were not measured. This PR keeps the upstream write-mode dispatch, including its partial-tile handling.

## Validation

The previously tested tail specialization passed 8,400 changing-input checks per rank at TP4 across BF16/FP16/FP32 and 600 per rank at TP2. The unmodified vLLM PR #58433 test file passed all four BF16/MXFP8 TP2/TP4 cases in 74.15 seconds. The unsafe release failed the reported shape at eager iteration 0, with 125 mismatches and a maximum absolute error of 22. The actual main-based branch and pristine `main` both clean-built for gfx950. All 48 gfx950 specialized read-kernel variants match the previously tested tail kernels byte-for-byte, including resource metadata; all 24 current-main read variants match the benchmarked #5694 baseline. All 24 PR write-kernel variants match pristine main. On the actual current-main PR branch, BF16/FP16/FP32 TP4 each passed six shapes with 100 eager and 100 graph iterations per shape. The unmodified vLLM integration suite passed again: **4 passed in 71.75 seconds**, covering BF16/MXFP8 at TP2/TP4. Ruff, Black, Python syntax, and diff checks passed.

Follow-up validation repeated the unchanged vLLM test group in **50 fresh pytest processes: 200/200 cases passed**, with zero failures, errors, skips, timeouts, or retries (68.2 minutes). Six runs emitted TCPStore shutdown warnings while all tests passed. The kernel and compiled collective library are unchanged by the benchmark-list follow-up.

The three boundary sizes also passed **18/18 cases through the existing benchmark** at TP4: BF16/FP16/FP32 in eager and graph modes. Profiler records confirmed the intended two-stage tail specialization for both neighbors and the aligned specialization for the middle size on all four ranks; 21 size-list/cutoff checks passed. These benchmark checks use the existing random-input tolerance. The default sweep now includes these shapes without `-s`, for example:

```bash
python op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_custom_allreduce.py -t 4 -d bf16 -m graph
```

"""Direct AITER TP4 latency/correctness study; host coordination uses Gloo."""

import argparse
import datetime
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import platform
import socket
import statistics
import time


def cases_for(args):
    cases = []
    for dtype in args.dtypes:
        element_size = 4 if dtype == "fp32" else 2
        candidates = []
        if args.case_set in ("all", "regression"):
            candidates += [(f"shape_{m}x512", (m, 512)) for m in (1023, 1024, 1025)]
        if args.case_set in ("all", "representative"):
            candidates += [(f"bytes_{n}", (n // element_size,))
                           for n in (8192, 65536, 262144, 524288, 1048576, 4194304, 8388608)]
        if args.case_set in ("all", "boundary"):
            candidates += [(f"tile_boundary_{offset:+}", ((1048576 + offset) // element_size,))
                           for offset in (-64, 0, 64, 63 * 64, 64 * 64, 65 * 64)]
        if args.case_set == "upstream":
            candidates += [(f"upstream_{m}x2880", (m, 2880))
                           for m in (120, 121, 127, 157, 160, 161, 256, 512)]
        seen = set()
        for name, shape in candidates:
            numel = 1
            for n in shape:
                numel *= n
            if numel in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(numel)
            cases.append({"name": name, "dtype": dtype, "shape": shape,
                          "bytes": numel * element_size, "numel": numel,
                          "full_packed_tile": numel * element_size % (512 * 16) == 0})
    return cases


def worker(rank, port, args):
    import torch
    import torch.distributed as dist
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
    device = torch.device("cuda", rank)
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", init_method=f"tcp://127.0.0.1:{port}",
                            rank=rank, world_size=4,
                            timeout=datetime.timedelta(seconds=60))
    from aiter.dist.device_communicators.custom_all_reduce import CustomAllreduce
    from aiter.jit import core
    ar = None
    report = {"config": vars(args), "results": []}
    try:
        ar = CustomAllreduce(dist.group.WORLD, device, max_size=16 * 1024 * 1024)
        assert not ar.disabled
        collective = Path(core.get_module("module_custom_all_reduce").__file__)
        report["metadata"] = {
            "python": platform.python_version(), "torch": torch.__version__,
            "device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(rank),
            "arch": torch.cuda.get_device_properties(rank).gcnArchName,
            "visible_devices": os.environ.get("HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES"),
            "collective": str(collective),
            "collective_sha256": hashlib.sha256(collective.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
        }
        dtype_map = {"bf16": torch.bfloat16, "fp16": torch.float16, "fp32": torch.float32}
        cases = cases_for(args)
        # Alternate case order as well as variant order across paired rounds.
        if args.reverse_cases:
            cases.reverse()
        for case in cases:
            x = torch.empty(case["shape"], dtype=dtype_map[case["dtype"]], device=device)
            indices = torch.arange(case["numel"], dtype=torch.int32, device=device).reshape(case["shape"])

            def set_input(seed):
                local = ((indices * (rank + 1) + seed * (rank + 3)) % 31) - 15
                x.copy_(local)
                ref = sum((((indices * (r + 1) + seed * (r + 3)) % 31) - 15)
                          for r in range(4))
                return ref.to(x.dtype)

            def check(outputs, expected):
                # Check every captured call: racing intermediate outputs also count.
                mismatch = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
                max_error = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
                finite = torch.ones((), dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
                for out in outputs:
                    mismatch += torch.count_nonzero(out != expected)
                    finite &= torch.isfinite(out).all()
                    max_error = torch.maximum(max_error, (out.float() - expected.float()).abs().max())
                return {"mismatches": mismatch.item(), "finite": finite.item(),
                        "max_abs_error": max_error.item()}

            for mode in args.modes:
                expected = set_input(1)
                for _ in range(args.warmup):
                    warm = ar.custom_all_reduce(x)
                    assert warm is not None
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
                dist.barrier()
                graph = None
                outputs = []
                if mode == "graph":
                    stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
                    stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
                    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
                    with ar.capture():
                        with torch.cuda.graph(graph, stream=stream):
                            outputs = [ar.custom_all_reduce(x) for _ in range(args.calls)]
                    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(stream)
                    for _ in range(args.warmup):
                        graph.replay()
                    torch.cuda.synchronize()
                    dist.barrier()

                timings = []
                wall_timings = []
                correctness = []
                start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
                end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
                for sample in range(args.samples):
                    expected = set_input(100 + sample)
                    if mode == "graph":
                        for out in outputs:
                            out.fill_(float("nan"))
                    torch.cuda.synchronize()
                    dist.barrier()
                    before = time.perf_counter()
                    start.record()
                    if mode == "graph":
                        for _ in range(args.replays):
                            graph.replay()
                        n_ops = args.calls * args.replays
                    else:
                        outputs = [ar.custom_all_reduce(x) for _ in range(args.calls)]
                        n_ops = args.calls
                    end.record()
                    end.synchronize()
                    wall_timings.append((time.perf_counter() - before) * 1e6 / n_ops)
                    timings.append(start.elapsed_time(end) * 1000 / n_ops)
                    correctness.append(check(outputs, expected))
                    dist.barrier()

                local = {"rank": rank, "samples_us": timings,
                         "median_us": statistics.median(timings),
                         "wall_samples_us": wall_timings,
                         "correctness": correctness}
                gathered = [None] * 4
                dist.all_gather_object(gathered, local)
                if rank == 0:
                    result = {**case, "mode": mode, "ranks": gathered,
                              "max_rank_median_us": max(r["median_us"] for r in gathered),
                              "exact": all(c["mismatches"] == 0 for r in gathered for c in r["correctness"]),
                              "finite": all(c["finite"] for r in gathered for c in r["correctness"])}
                    report["results"].append(result)
                    destination = Path(args.output)
                    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                    temporary = destination.with_suffix(".tmp")
                    temporary.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n")
                    temporary.replace(destination)
                    print(f"RESULT {case['dtype']} {case['name']} {mode} "
                          f"us={result['max_rank_median_us']:.4f} "
                          f"exact={result['exact']} finite={result['finite']}", flush=True)
                del outputs, graph
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
                dist.barrier()
            del x, indices, expected, warm
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        dist.barrier()
    finally:
        if ar is not None:
            ar.close()
        dist.destroy_process_group()


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--dtypes", nargs="+", choices=("bf16", "fp16", "fp32"),
                        default=["bf16", "fp16", "fp32"])
    parser.add_argument("--modes", nargs="+", choices=("eager", "graph"), default=["eager", "graph"])
    parser.add_argument("--case-set", choices=("all", "regression", "representative", "boundary", "upstream"), default="all")
    parser.add_argument("--calls", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--replays", type=int, default=10)
    parser.add_argument("--samples", type=int, default=7)
    parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--reverse-cases", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--list-cases", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    assert min(args.calls, args.replays, args.samples, args.warmup) > 0
    return args


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = parse_args()
    if args.list_cases:
        print(json.dumps(cases_for(args), indent=2))
    else:
        import torch.multiprocessing as mp
        with socket.socket() as sock:
            sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
            port = sock.getsockname()[1]
        mp.spawn(worker, args=(port, args), nprocs=4, join=True)

## History and motivation

This work began when [vLLM PR #58433](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58433) intermittently failed TP4 tests in [Buildkite build #90750](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/90750) despite passing on retry. Routing partial messages to the naive kernel restored correctness but increased BF16 graph latency by about 29%. Merged [AITER PR #5694](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5694) fixes the barrier defect with uniform loop bounds. This follow-up retains its write-mode and fused fixes while specializing complete tiles and leftover packs in the plain read kernel. The motivation is to preserve the correctness fix with minimal performance cost and keep the original test shapes and assertions.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Tune gfx1201 unified attention 2d for D=512 for full attention and D=256 for Sliding Window (Gemma4 shapes) and fix D=1024 launches
body:
## Motivation

Improve unified-attention prefill on Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201) for Gemma-4-31B shapes (full attention D=512, sliding attention D=256), including fp8 KV cache, and fix `attn_2d` launch failures for head sizes that pad to 1024.

On `main`, gfx1201 `attn_2d` is keyed only on Q and dtype. Any head size from 513 to 1024 at Q ≥ 256 gets BLOCK_M=64 / TILE=32, but the kernel allocates tiles for `HEAD_SIZE_PADDED = next_power_of_2(head_size)` = 1024. That requests 128 KiB of LDS against the 64 KiB limit, so D=576, 768 and 1024 fail to launch.

## Technical Details

**Root cause.** The kernel sizes its tiles for `next_power_of_2(head_size)`, but `attn_2d` configs were chosen by the raw head size. On `main`, every head from 513 to 1024 at Q ≥ 256 gets BLOCK_M=64 / TILE=32 at width 1024, which needs 128 KiB of LDS (limit 64 KiB) and fails to launch.

**Fix: power-of-two `D_LEQ_*` bands**, the encoding used in [#4868](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4868). Because `D ≤ 2ⁿ` which is `next_power_of_2(D) ≤ 2ⁿ`, each band's config is sized for the width it runs at.

| Head size (pads to) | `attn_2d` entries |
|---|---|
| ≤ 128 | existing entries, copied verbatim (routing unchanged) |
| 129–256 | tuned per dtype for Q ≥ 64, plus one bf16 sliding entry (`num_stages=2`) |
| 257–512 | tuned per dtype for Q ≥ 64 |
| 513–1024 | LDS guard for Q ≥ 256: BLOCK_M=32, TILE=16, 8 warps |
| > 1024 | unchanged |

**Tuning.** Configs come from a sweep of 132 workloads × 50 configs over D, Q, K, sliding window and dtype. Only D and dtype change the best config. K does not, one config wins for every Q from 64 to 2048, and sliding matters only for D=256 bf16 (~3%). So there is no K axis, a single Q threshold at 64, and separate fp8 entries.

**Benchmark fix.** `bench_unified_attention.py -test` passed the unquantized tensors plus the fp8 descales to `ref_paged_attn`, which then applied the descale a second time, so every fp8 run printed FAIL. It now passes the tensors the kernel receives. bf16 runs are unchanged.

`test_unified_attention_config.py` checks that every head size gets the config of its padded width and fits LDS, and pins the gfx1201 routes. It reads the JSON without a GPU, so it runs in CI; it fails on main's table.

## Test Plan

- `git diff --check`; JSON validation.
- Routing check against `main`'s table: D ≤ 128 and D > 1024 must route identically for every Q (1–299 and larger), sliding on/off, and dtype pair; heads 129–1024 must land in the band of their padded width.
-  `python -m pytest -q op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_unified_attention_config.py`
- `python -m pytest -q op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_unified_attention.py -k '2048'`.
- `bench_unified_attention.py -test` (with the fixed reference) on 119 targeted cases: Q ∈ {63, 64, 255, 256, 1025} × D ∈ {256, 512} × full/sliding × {bf16, fp8 KV, fp8}; D ∈ {128, 192, 384, 576, 768, 1024} × Q ∈ {64, 255, 256, 1024} × full/sliding; the performance shapes below.
- Performance: `main`'s JSON vs this JSON on the same source, median of 5 trials after prewarm, alternating order.

## Test Result

- Routing check: passed.
- pytest `-k '2048'`: **512 passed**, 1536 skipped, 2144 deselected. Skips are Gluon/shuffled-cache paths unavailable on gfx1201; deselected are the `num_blocks=32768` cases, which exceed this 32 GiB GPU's memory.
- Targeted cases: **119/119 passed** the reference check, including all fp8 cases. D=576, 768 and 1024 now launch; `main` fails them with 128 KiB vs 64 KiB LDS.
- Benchmark fix: fp8 max_diff drops from 0.42–0.44 (FAIL) to 0.002–0.011 (PASS); bf16 and `-fp8_output` results are unchanged.

Performance (ms, BF16 unless noted; HQ=32; D=512: HK=4, page 64; D=256: HK=16, page 32, window 1024):

| Workload | `main` | This PR | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Full D=512, Q=256, K=1024 | 1.535 | **0.453** | 3.39× |
| Full D=512, Q=1024, K=8192 | 52.20 | **14.12** | 3.70× |
| Full D=512, Q=1024, K=8192, fp8 KV | 100.38 | **24.81** | 4.05× |
| Full D=512, Q=128, K=8192 | 7.101 | **1.997** | 3.56× |
| Sliding D=256, Q=1024, K=8192 | 0.734 | **0.642** | 1.14× |
| Sliding D=256, Q=1024, K=8192, fp8 KV | 1.573 | **1.191** | 1.32× |
| Sliding D=256, Q=128, K=8192 | 0.197 | **0.099** | 1.99× |
| Full D=1024, Q=1024, K=4096 | fails (LDS) | **44.99** | now launches |

These are kernel timings for batch size 1, not end-to-end model throughput.

**Known limitation (pre-existing, unchanged).** The wrapper raises `BLOCK_M` to `next_power_of_2(HQ/HK)` after the config lookup, so very high GQA ratios (64 atD=1024, 128 at D ≥ 512) exceed LDS on `main` and with this table alike; a JSON entry cannot prevent it, and it needs a wrapper change. Ratio 32 at D=1024 nowlaunches (`main` fails).

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Bugfix][MLA] Mask the >2GB global_load path in mla_gluon decode (fixes gfx950 IMA)
body:
## Problem
On gfx950, serving **Kimi-K2.6** (8 heads/rank @ TP8, `kv_lora_rank=512`, bf16 KV) with vLLM crashes at decode warmup with a GPU **illegal memory access** inside the Gluon MLA decode kernel (`mla_gluon`). Its paged KV cache is far larger than 2 GB, so the wrapper sets `within_2gb=False` and KV is loaded via `global_load_to_shared` (64-bit offsets) instead of `buffer_load_to_shared`.

## Root cause
The `>2GB` `global_load_to_shared` calls (the `else` of each `if WITHIN_2GB:`) dropped the bounds `mask` that their `buffer_load_to_shared` siblings carry. A partial split block then dereferences out-of-bounds KV rows -> IMA. Additionally, `buffer_load` returns `0` for masked lanes while `global_load` leaves them undefined, so a mask alone yields **NaNs** on partial blocks -- `other=0.0` is required to match `buffer_load` semantics.

Introduced by #4474 (which added the int64 `>2GB` global_load path); still present on current `main`.

## Fix
Add `mask=<same predicate as the buffer_load sibling>, other=0.0` to all 8 `global_load_to_shared` calls in `_mla_gluon`.

## Test
Adds `test_mla_gluon_decode_over_2gb` to `op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_mla.py`: it drives a >2 GB cache through the `global_load` path and asserts finiteness + bit-parity against the `<2GB` `buffer_load` reference on identical KV.

The two configs are chosen so that **every one of the 8 masked loads is executed**, keyed on `num_iter = cdiv(per_split, BLOCK_N=64)` with `per_split = max(64, ctx // NUM_KV_SPLITS)` and `NUM_KV_SPLITS = min(256 // batch, cdiv(ctx, 64))` (bh16bn64 regime):

| config | NUM_KV_SPLITS | per_split | num_iter | loads exercised |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `(batch=8, ctx=777)` | 13 | 64 | 1 | prologue loads, last split is a **partial** block (mask + `other=0.0`) |
| `(batch=4, ctx=33000)` | 64 | 515 | 9 | prologue + **loop-body** loads + **epilogue** load (partial tail = 3) |

So `(4, 33000)` reaches `for i in range(num_iter - 2)` and the `if num_iter >= 2` epilogue — the paths a `num_iter == 1` config never touches.

```
pytest op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_mla.py -k test_mla_gluon_decode_over_2gb
```

The fix itself was validated on MI350 (gfx950): the >2 GB path output matches the `buffer_load` reference (`max_abs_diff=0.0`), the standalone repro goes from memory-access-fault -> clean, and **Kimi-K2.6 `-tp 8` serves** on upstream vLLM.

AI assistance was used; changes were human-reviewed.

title: [FlyDSL] Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate
body:
# Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate

The decode path now has four candidate kernels and no single one wins the shape space, so this adds the kernel behind a table of measured row intervals keyed by `(arch, CU count, emit, k, width)`. An `(arch, CU count)` pair the table does not name keeps today's behaviour exactly.

## How the dispatch works

Three public entry points reach the decode path, and they do not share a call chain: `topk_select()` routes its `decode` arm, and `aiter.flydsl_top_k_per_row_decode()` its whole call, straight into the FlyDSL host, never passing through `top_k_per_row_decode()`. So the gate sits in both places, both ask one function rather than deciding for themselves, and neither takes a backend from its caller, which is what keeps them from disagreeing about a shape.

```
  top_k_per_row_decode()              topk_select()                aiter.flydsl_top_k_per_row_decode()
  aiter/ops/topk.py                   aiter/ops/topk_select.py     aiter/ops/topk.py
          |                              |- argmax / small_k / plain         |
          |                              |- stream                           |
          |                              \- decode                           |
          |                                   |                              |
          |                                   v                              |
          |                     flydsl_top_k_per_row_decode()  <-------------+
          |                     aiter/ops/flydsl/topk/topk_per_row.py
          |                                   |
    [gate here]                         [gate here]
          |                                   |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
                            v
              decode_backend_for_call()   <- the only decision
                            |
     +----------------------+---------------------+
     v                      v                     v
  adaptive               chunked              upstream
  (in a band of          (in upstream's       (not ours; the dispatch
   the measured           chunked gate,        below picks the port
   table, looked up       read at the          where enabled, else the
   at the live length)    physical width)      HIP/C++ kernel)
```

The gate never names the fallback kernel itself: it answers "not ours" and upstream's existing dispatch picks, which is the port on gfx950 and gfx1250 and the HIP/C++ kernel elsewhere. That is also why a caller wanting values never reaches the adaptive kernel, which emits indices only. Only `top_k_per_row_decode()` has that dispatch below it. In `topk_select()` the decode arm is already chosen, so "not ours" leaves the chunked kernel.

## `max_row_len`, and what a caller has to pass

A decode buffer is allocated once at the model's maximum context and a call fills whatever part of it the requests need. `seq_lens` is device-resident, so the host cannot read it without a sync, and the adaptive kernel picks its tier, part count and workspace on the host before launch. Given only the buffer, it builds a short row as if it were a full one.

So the new argument states the longest live row in the batch. A serving stack that assembles the batch already has it -- it is `max(seqLens)`. No caller in aiter passes it yet, so nothing reaches the new kernel until a stack opts in. The tables below declare it.

- **It is a guarantee, not a hint.** Part of what it selects is compiled in, so a bound below the longest live row returns wrong indices rather than merely slower ones. It cannot be checked here without the sync this path exists to avoid. A bound above it is always correct; it only costs the win.
- **`None` declines the adaptive kernel and nothing else.** The chunked bands keep reading the physical width they were fitted on, so a call that passes nothing routes exactly where it routes today.
- **It never changes a result**, only which kernel produces it.

## Results

Every cell is scored, not only the ones the gate takes. A band takes a cell when the kernel is no slower than the best of the four and at least 1.05x faster than what runs there today; a smaller margin is noise. Every entry had to satisfy that on **both** slices below, so a cell that only clears it on the diagonal is not in the table. Nothing is behind on either slice.

A ratio is today's kernel over this PR's, so a declined cell is 1.00x by construction and the geomean covers every cell. Each card's own grid and per-cell winners are below.

Protocol: all four arms are timed the same way on every cell, under graph replay, and the cell's number is the median over its repeats; cells where the arms came out close were re-timed with more.

**On the diagonal**, where the buffer is exactly full.

body:
## Motivation
 
FlashKDA still spoke a dense ABI: `initial_state[N, H, V, K]` plus a freshly allocated `out`. vLLM Kimi-K3 serving keeps recurrent state in a paged pool `[slots, H, V, K]` with `state_indices` / `has_initial_state`.

Wiring that through AITER meant:
 
1. `gather_initial_states` (or `state_cache[indices]`) into a dense tensor

2. run `chunk_kimi_delta_attn`

3. scatter `final_state` back

4. `out.copy_(kernel_out)`
 
Those copies sit in the serving timer. On MI350, a K3-shaped FlashKDA prefill paid ~40–60 µs for them (4K: 171 → 130 µs, 16K: 499 → 440 µs with the same segment pin). The fused vLLM path already reads and writes the pool in-kernel ([vLLM #54038](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54038)); this PR gives FlashKDA the same cache contract so a later vLLM dispatch ([#56036](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56036)) does not have to gather around AITER.

 
## Technical Details
 
Public kwargs on `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` / `flash_kda_fwd`:
 
- `state_cache`: fp32 V-first `[slots, H, V, K]`. Each slot plane is dense; `stride(0)` may pad.

- `state_indices`: int32 `[N]`

- `has_initial_state`: bool `[N]`; false starts that sequence from zero and does not read a dirty slot

- `out`: required with `state_cache`, same shape as `v` (K2 still loads `v`, so `out` must not alias it)
 
K2 and the scan load/store `slot * stride(0) + head * V * K + …`. The last segment writes the final state back to the same row. Segmented pass A does not bind `state_cache` (keeps the existing K2 binary / autotune; binding it here previously ~2× slowed K2).
 
`@input_guard(skip=("state_cache",))` leaves the pool’s storage and `stride(0)` alone. Other operands are still packed. The skip is an AITER decorator default, not a vLLM flag; the caller just passes `state_cache=` as a keyword.
 
Dense `initial_state` is unchanged and mutually exclusive with `state_cache`. `final_state` is `None` when the cache is used.
 
The default five-kernel path indexes a dense `h0` and is GVA / C=64 / K-first. If `state_cache` is set and FlashKDA is not selected,

`chunk_delta_attn_fwd` raises instead of ignoring the argument.
 
 
## Test Plan
 
```bash

pytest op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda.py \

  -k 'paged_cache or flash_kda' -q

```
 
Added cases:
 
- `test_paged_cache_matches_dense` — paged vs dense `initial_state`, bit-identical `out` and selected slots; empty slots untouched; unsegmented and segmented

- `test_paged_cache_has_initial_state_false` — false flag matches a zero `initial_state`

- `test_paged_cache_padded_stride_writes_live_pool` — non-contiguous `stride(0)` updates the original storage pointer

- `test_paged_cache_rejected_on_default_pipeline` — non-FlashKDA call with `state_cache` raises
 
Serving-shaped A/B (K3 H=12, D=128, `lower_bound=-5`, varlen `cu_seqlens`)

vs gather and vs vLLM fused prefill on gfx950.
 
## Test Result
 
Paged vs dense FlashKDA: `torch.equal` on output and selected cache rows (rel err 0).
 
Paged FlashKDA vs vLLM fused prefill (same op, not e2e): output rel L2 ~4.8e-3, state ~2.5e-3 at 4K/16K.
 
MI350X, official vLLM ROCm image, serving-style call (µs, smaller is better):

 
| shape | gather FlashKDA | paged FlashKDA | fused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1×4096, H=12 | 171 | **130** | 125 |
| 1×16384, H=12, `--segment 8` | 499 | **440** | 389 |
| 1×16384, H=12, auto segment | — | **380** | 388 |

 
Default-pipeline reject and padded-stride tests pass.

## Motivation

<!-- Explain the purpose of this PR and the goals it aims to achieve. -->
This PR adds  Triton Conv3D implementation with optimized
routing for common video-model and VAE workloads.

The public API supports FP16 and BF16 inputs, NCDHW and channels-last-3D
execution, optional bias, asymmetric stride/padding/dilation, and activations.
## Technical Details

The Conv3D router selects between the following kernel families:

- Specialized 1x1x1 Conv3D
- NCDHWc 3x3x3 Conv3D with fused activation packing
- Native NDHWC 3x3x3 Conv3D
- General im2col-free Conv3D
- Winograd F(4x4, 3x3) over the H/W axes
- Winograd with an NCDHWc input path

The implementation also adds:

- Conv3D weight-prepack and Winograd-filter caches
- Layout-preserving NCDHW and channels-last-3D behavior
- Shape-driven production routing
- Complete launch keys containing all three spatial axes
- Tuned gfx1201 launch configurations
- Configuration-table coverage for gfx1200, gfx942, and gfx950, initially
  seeded from the gfx1201 values
- Public export through `aiter.ops.triton`
- Real-model-derived benchmark shape coverage for:
  - Wan2.2 A14B VAE
  - Wan2.2 TI2V-5B VAE
  - LTX-Video 0.9.5 VAE
  - InternVideo2 and Qwen-family video patch embeddings

The benchmark reports per-layer correctness, selected Triton kernels,
kernel-only and repack-inclusive performance, aggregate throughput, and
call-count-weighted encoder/decoder totals. It exits nonzero when a requested
shape errors or fails correctness.

<!-- Explain the changes along with any relevant GitHub links. -->

## Test Plan

The Conv3D test suite covers:

- FP16 and BF16
- NCDHW and channels-last-3D layouts
- Every direct Conv3D route
- Optional bias
- `none`, `relu`, `relu6`, and `gelu` activations
- Asymmetric dimensions, stride, padding, and dilation
- Batched, odd-channel, and tail-masking shapes
- Winograd transform and output correctness
- Output dtype preservation
- Weight-cache reuse, invalidation, and LRU eviction
- Actual production-router dispatch
- Benchmark database, reporting, and CLI behavior
- Invalid argument and unsupported configuration handling

Tests were run on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (`gfx1201`) after clearing the
Triton compilation cache.

```text

```
